Setting the Stage for EdTech Pilots in Special Education

An edtech pilot refers to the preliminary trial implementation of technology tools within educational environments aimed at assessing their impact, usability, and scalability. This crucial pilot phase allows educators and admins to explore whether a technology solution aligns with the needs and operational dynamics before committing to full-scale, districtwide adoption.

Just as in a general education setting, launching an edtech pilot for special education populations involves meticulous planning and alignment with district-specific educational goals. It's crucial that district and school stakeholders collaboratively define these objectives to ensure the technology addresses their unique needs. Here's how to establish clear, impactful objectives for an special education edtech pilot and effectively evaluate the results:

Defining Pilot Objectives:

Stakeholder Workshops: Initiate the pilot planning with some informal workshops that encompass all impacted stakeholders—general education teachers, special education teachers, related service providers (like speech therapists and occupational therapists), IT staff, administrators, and when feasible, students and their parents. Take advantage of pre-established internal team meetings, and invite members of your tech team to join. If a live workshop isn't feasible, craft a thoughtful survey to gather insights and expectations from all stakeholders, in order to ensure your pilot objectives meet the diverse needs of everyone who will interact with or benefit from the edtech tool.

Needs Assessment: Perform a targeted needs assessment specific to special education, examining current resources, educator workloads, and the unique challenges faced by students with special needs. This assessment should identify gaps in technology, accessibility, and instructional support that the edtech solution aims to fill.

Alignment with District Goals: Align the objectives of the edtech pilot with the district's specific goals for special education, such as improving individualized educational outcomes, enhancing adaptive learning technologies, or facilitating more effective intervention strategies. Ensure these goals reflect the aspirations and compliance requirements of special education programs within the district.

Evaluating the Impact on Educators:

Educator Feedback: Throughout the pilot, you should plan to solicit feedback from both general and special education teachers. Focus on how the edtech tool impacts their instructional methods and administrative tasks, particularly in terms of reducing workload and enhancing the delivery of differentiated instruction. Soliciting this feedback isn't something that should fall squarely on your or your staff's shoulders – the best edtech vendors will work alongside you to systematically collect insights on how the tool being piloted is influencing your educators' work.

Observational Studies: Conduct classroom observations to assess how the technology fits into the daily teaching activities in special education settings. Observe its usability, accessibility, and effectiveness in engaging students with various learning needs and how it supports teachers and related service providers in managing diverse classrooms. When evaluating edtech vendors, ensure you have a solid understanding of how they'll support you in assessing the tool's impact.

Evaluating the Impact on Students:

Performance Metrics: Establish specific performance metrics that reflect the educational goals for students with special needs. These might include progress in personalized learning targets, improvement in specific skill sets as outlined in their IEPs, or better engagement and interaction with learning materials.

Student Surveys and Feedback: Collect feedback from students participating in the pilot, using methods and tools adapted for their specific communication and understanding levels. Ensure that their direct experiences with the technology are documented and considered in the pilot evaluation.

Assessing the Vendor Partnership:

Support Quality: Critically evaluate the vendor's capability to meet the specialized needs of special education, including the provision of robust training that addresses the unique challenges of special education settings, and the responsiveness to specialized support requests.

Resource Availability: Assess whether the vendor provides high-quality, adaptable resources that can be customized to support a wide range of disabilities and learning challenges. These resources should support the goals of special education and comply with educational standards and regulations.

Expertise of Vendor Staff: Consider the expertise of the vendor's team, particularly whether they have former educators with domain-specific knowledge who guide the development and implementation of the product. The presence of staff with hands-on experience in special education can significantly enhance the relevance and effectiveness of the technology.

Evidence Basis of the Product: Evaluate the scientific and educational foundation of the edtech tool. Ensure that there is credible evidence supporting its efficacy in the context of special education. This assessment helps guarantee that the product is not only innovative but also effective in real-world educational settings.

Challenges and Solutions in EdTech Pilots

Implementing edtech in both general and special education settings presents unique challenges. Understanding these obstacles and preparing solutions in advance can greatly enhance the success of an edtech pilot. Here, we explore common challenges along with strategies to address them, ensuring smoother implementations across different educational spheres.

Solution: Prioritize vendors who offer robust integration capabilities and have a track record of successful implementations with similar school systems. Conduct a pilot phase that specifically tests integration points and work closely with IT staff to monitor data flow and system interactions.

Training and Professional Development:

Challenge: Both general and special education teachers may feel hesitant to adopt and/or face steep learning curves with new technologies. Without proper training, the adoption of the tool can be slow, and its effectiveness diminished.

Solution: Develop a comprehensive training program tailored to the specific needs of educators. Include hands-on sessions, continuous support, and feedback mechanisms. Ensure your vendor partner has a robust plan for supporting your district's professional development efforts, as it relates to the technology tool.

Budget Constraints:

Solution: Explore various funding sources, including grants, federal funding, and partnerships with edtech companies. Consider phased implementations to spread out costs over time.

Measuring Impact and Success:

Challenge: Defining and measuring the success of an edtech tool can be complex, with varying metrics for success in general and special education.

Solution: Establish clear, measurable objectives at the outset of the pilot. Use a mix of qualitative and quantitative data to assess impact, including student performance metrics, user satisfaction surveys, and direct observation.

By anticipating these challenges and preparing appropriate solutions, districts can ensure that their edtech pilots are more likely to succeed, bringing valuable technological advancements to both general and special education settings.

The potential of these online courses/ programmes to provide educational access to all has generated significant interest among students, academicians and executives in corporate world. There are various reasons for such dropouts. Lack of time, boring course, less learner engagement are some of the reasons. Though MOOC developers cannot do much about dropout due to issues related to learners' issues such as lack of time or lack of support, they can definitely work towards improving learner engagement and improving learning experience. Research provides enough evidence for the strong positive link between higher learner engagement and retention in online courses.

What is learner engagement and why it is important?

Learner engagement refers to the degree of interest, curiosity, attention and passion that learners show when they are learning or being taught.

In online learning environment, engaging learners is quite a challenge. Learner engagement concept is based on the belief that learning improves significantly when learners are inquisitive, interested, or inspired, whereas learning tends to suffer when students are bored, dispassionate, disaffected, or otherwise "disengage".

Is there a way to engage learners?

There are different ways to keep learners engaged in online learning environment. For instance, enabling learners to monitor their own progress motivates them to achieve course goals. Another example of engaging learners is to set achievable goals in the course. This encourages them to become self-motivated and independent learners.

Previous research that examined traditional online courses has suggested several factors that could influence student engagement. These factors include instructor presence, instructor humour, availability of feedback, choice of activities, extra course resources and active learning.

Let us see how have we tried to engage learners in IIMBx MOOCs.

What is IIMBx doing to engage learners?

IIMBx team consistently works towards improving learner engagement. All courses comprise lecture videos, text components and discussions and they act as core / standard learning components and not as additional components for engagement. Here we list few instances of learner engagement practices used in IIMBx MOOCs.

Interviews: One of the most powerful techniques we have in digital learning is the ability to interview subject matter experts. Interviews can be considered as a different flavour that we provide not only to enhance knowledge but also to help in engaging the learners.

Characters and interaction with them: Introducing 'Characters' in MOOCs helps learners have a kind of 'break' from watching monotonous lecture videos. These characters bring 'joyful moments' without deviating from the topic in discussion. The Lysa character in "Statistics for Business", the Dude and Nerd character in the course "Predictive Analytics", the Guru character in the course "Innovation and IT Management" and the Trigger and Clever character in the course "Financial Accounting and Analysis" are some of the examples of usage of characters in IIMBx MOOCs.

Image: Example of usage of Characters

Animations (Video): Animation videos can act as a tool of learner engagement if they are well-made, relevant and crisp. Stories and Scenarios can be depicted in a much better way through animated videos. These kinds of videos help in grabbing the attention of learners and help them to connect with the core content. We have used these kind of animation videos in courses like Accounting for Decision Making, Organizational Design, etc.

Image: Example of usage of Animation videos

Notes: By introducing 'notes', we try to help learners take note of points that learners feel important to learn, remember or recall later. All the notes taken can be accessed at one place making it easy for learners to learn effectively.

Infographics: Sometimes it may be necessary to remember certain stages of a process or steps of a procedure or certain complicated task. It may be important to remember some data or statistics. Using mere text components or videos to illustrate these may not be sufficient. This is where 'infographics' help. Infographics are graphic visual representations of information, data or knowledge intended to present information clearly. They help in simplifying the information in a visually engaging way in order to attract and inform learners. These infographics are particularly useful for learners who are less likely to remember text-based walkthroughs. It not only simplifies complex concepts or ideas and helps increase retention but also helps digest information and make your course content interesting. A number of IIMBx courses contain infographics to depict a certain content, share knowledge and provide additional information. For instance, infographics are used in courses such as "Healthcare in India: A strategic perspectives", "Customer Relationship Management", etc.

Image: Example of Infographics in IIMBx courses

Self-Assessment Questions: Self-assessment questions play a significant role as a learning tool in MOOCs. These are questions designed for learners to assess their own understanding of the concepts. Self-Assessment Questions have lots of benefits. They encourage learner involvement and responsibility. They help learners to think about their own learning and learning progress. In addition, when learners are able to analyze their own progress, they can find ways, or strategies to make improvements.

All IIMBx courses have self-assessment questions. These questions are not restricted by number of attempts. Hence learners can find out the correct answers. Our course survey indicates that learners find these self-assessment questions quite useful.

Audio Podcast: Some of our IIMBx courses contain audio podcasts as learning components. Audio podcast is a digital audio file that is created, shared and heard. They are great alternatives for delivering course content. These podcasts can hugely benefit auditory learners and help them in their learning. A big advantage of audio podcast is the attention it attracts. While text and video require learners to pay full attention in order to consume the content, audio podcasts can be used to learn concepts without much difficulty. Learners need not sit at one place to consume the content. They can listen to the audio while driving, while travelling by bus, while cooking or while washing the dishes.

We have used audio podcasts in some of our IIMBx courses such as Customer Relationship Management and Introduction to People Management and our learners find it extremely convenient to learn through these audio podcasts.

Interactive elements: Some of our courses contain interactive elements such as exploration exercises (from Oppia) and interactive visual display boards. Explorations are interactive elements that help learners to learn concepts in a fun and a creative way using images, text and questions. It can act as a wonderful tool for self-learning. You can find these exploration exercises in our course on Marketing Management.

Another interactive element which we have used is the visual display boards. These boards allow course creators to display content in different forms (text, audio, video, etc.) under one roof. Such display boards can be used for many purposes such as introducing a lesson or summarizing a concept. We have used these display boards in Customer Relationship Management course.

What we didn't include in our metrics
Cost
MOOC platforms each have unique ways of monetizing their courses, so we couldn't adequately compare cost between platforms. For instance, some charge a monthly subscription fee, while others provide some free courses and charge a fee for those that are more popular or for "specializations." There are even some that allow you to audit the course for free, but you won't get any sort of certificate without paying.
Whatever the pricing model, MOOCs are almost always an order of magnitude cheaper than equivalent courses at a university. For instance, a full course in VR from Udacity costs $1,200, while studying for a graduate degree from Stanford could cost upward of $30,000 in one year. Of course, the value of a Stanford degree would be higher than a certification from Udacity, but the comparison in price shows how relatively inexpensive MOOCs typically are.
Paying for a MOOC isn't always a bad thing because those who pay for a course have a tendency to be more engaged in the material. Additionally, those who pay also tend to have lower dropout rates than those who don't.
Ease of use
We measured aspects that improve the user experience, such as:
The number of search filters (to make finding relevant courses easier)
The number of languages courses are available in and the number of languages available in video subtitles
Whether each platform has a fully functional mobile app
Success or completion rate
Traditionally, critics of the MOOC model have pointed out the astronomical dropout rate for MOOCs. A retention rate of 10% is widely cited which means that 90% of those who sign up for a MOOC don't earn a certificate of completion.

Is the goal simply to get students to complete a course and receive a certificate at the end? According to this study from Harvard, many learners don't even intend to obtain a certificate of completion when they start the course. Other goals may exist, like:
Investigating whether a certain field or subject is interesting to the particular student
Gaining a rough understanding of multiple subjects
Learning about a single concept within a MOOC
For those reasons, we decided that completion rate isn't a useful indicator of a MOOC's quality.
The quality of individual MOOCs within the platforms
This guide focuses on ranking the platforms, not the individual courses. It's important to note that one course on a platform that didn't score well overall may be of a higher quality than another course on a different platform that ranked near the top.

In 2011, Sebastian Thrun co-taught an Artificial Intelligence course with Peter Norvig of Google at Stanford. They made it available for free online. Over 150,000 students from 190 countries signed up, along with the several hundred Stanford students on campus.
Impressed, he left Stanford to co-found Udacity and make courses available online in a massive scale. In his words:
"Having done this, I can't teach at Stanford again."
Another Stanford professor, Andrew Ng, had a similar experience teaching a Machine Learning course online. 104,000 people enrolled from around the globe. He co-founded Coursera, a similar organization to Udacity, noting:
"It would take me 250 years to teach this many people at Stanford."
The courses available from Coursera and Udacity, along with edX and universities themselves, are called MOOCs: massive, open, online courses. They are free and open to anyone. If you enroll, there are assignments, tests, and even final exams that you will need to pass to complete the course.
MOOCs have exploded in popularity, but one criticism has been low rate at which people complete the courses. Sebastian Thrun has been quoted as being "deeply concerned by the 90% dropout rate," while Daphne Koller of Coursera described a retention rate of 7% to 9% in their courses.
While their enrollment numbers are impressive, the concern is that MOOCs aren't effectively educating people on the promised scale. As Thrun says, "MOOCS will only succeed if they make normally motivated students successful."
But to what should these 10% completion rates be compared? The completion rate of traditional courses? To this authors' knowledge, this data is not widely available. One standard is the federal government's financial aid requirement that students complete 67% of the units they attempt. By that metric, MOOCs perform poorly. But the actual completion rate may fall below 67% in practice.
Besides, many people "enrolling" in MOOCs do so simply to get a sense of the course. The marginal cost of trying a MOOC is practically zero. It's like piling a bunch of deserts on your plate at an all-you-can-eat buffet. Do you really expect to finish them all? This author, for example, once enrolled in 6 Coursera courses in a day just to choose one to take. Commentators note that a majority of enrollees likely sign up to watch the lectures and never intend to complete any course assignments.
MOOCs are relatively new, so it's not surprising that their impact is hard to judge. But one thing is for certain, the higher education industry that they're targeting is ripe for disruption. Tuition costs are up, students hold over $1 trillion in student loans, and, as reported by The New York Times blog Economix, graduation rates from American universities are unimpressive.

Question: What is the approximate dropout rate in MOOCs, according to Sebastian Thrun? Answer: 90%

Question: Which of the following is NOT a reason why people might enroll in MOOCs? A) To complete the course B) To get a sense of the course C) To watch lectures D) To choose one course out of many. Answer: A) To complete the course (as many people enroll just to get a sense of the course or watch lectures)

Answer: Coursera", "truncated": false, "original_chars": 3393, "returned_chars": 3393}, {"rank": 8, "id": "shard_01935_10105", "docid": "shard_01935_10105", "kind": "document", "rrf_score": 0.020417, "text": "Since their inception, there has been a flurry of debate around the legitimacy and efficacy of MOOCs (Massive Open Online Courses). Widely recognized as game-changing in education, they offer radical reach and democratize access to education unlike anything we've ever seen. However, the rise of anything new and exciting is typically accompanied by criticism. In the case of MOOCs, it has been heavy. Skeptics point to uncertainty in scalability, assessment, engagement — the list goes on.

The main argument being made against MOOCs attacks the perceived lack of success as measured by their low completion rates (Mass MOOC Dropouts). The interpretation of this metric varies greatly.

Critics are obsessed with the infamous five percent rate, pointing out that "If 95 percent of students who enrolled in a residential college course dropped out or failed, that course would rightly be considered a disaster."

Some take it further (the MOOC Racket), claiming that MOOCs are a platform for evangelizing academic rock stars to the detriment of students and teachers, and arguing that educators can't teach tens of thousands of people at once — "that MOOCs only deliver information, but that's not education."

What is clear from all the fur flying is that people aren't satisfied with the current state of affairs in U.S. education. But are MOOCs really failing to make the grade? Is this the right interpretation of that troubling five percent?

As a technologist, I look at the five percent through a very different lens than educators do. Equating online conversion rates to offline behavior is naive, and any attempt to hold MOOCs to a classroom standard for learning is going to lead to disappointment.

Examined through conversion rates, one of the Web's favorite metrics, five percent is very typical for early Web companies. Through this lens, our criticism of MOOCs instantly transforms into a relatively average complaint. Does this mean that MOOCs are right where they should be for a nascent technology? That's a question worth asking.

The other group we really haven't heard from in this debate is students. Sure, we have the infamous "five percent completers," but do educators really know what's going on in the heads of the other students?

The answer is no.

The instruments educators are currently using to measure them don't tell much of anything. For example, time spent watching online video, which seems to be the measurement of choice, if not one of the only measurements of engagement for MOOCs, is a blunt instrument.

Technologists would look at the problem differently. We love data, and as much of it as we can get. And by creating interaction with learners, we could capture data that shows different types of engagement, and whether or not people are actually learning from MOOCs, a question that I don't believe has been adequately addressed up until now.

Measuring engagement could come in many different forms that educators haven't explored yet. For example, by intersecting MOOCs with adaptive learning or gaming, we could capture a phenomenal amount of data and have the added benefit of improving how people learn, and how well they remember information. One could also measure rates of learning and forgetting, and effectiveness of content being taught on a very granular level, and ultimately provide instructors with insight into how their content is performing. This, in turn, will let them improve the process or intervene with students when needed.

Before we pass judgement, we need to look at MOOCs again, this time from all angles, and start digging for contextualized data to serve as the foundation for evaluation.

Our education system is in dire need of positive change, and while MOOC 1.0 is not a panacea for what ails the system, the interest in online learning and the fiery arguments around the subject suggest that there's something here worth exploring further.

If properly channeled — and combined with a bit of forward thinking — I believe MOOC 2.0 will make the grade, and be the game-changer we're all hoping for.

Andrew Smith Lewis is founder and executive chairman of the memory-management tool Cerego. He spoke last week at SXSW EDU and SXSW Interactive about "Hardwiring the Brain" and improving experiences in education. Follow him @aslives.

A practical design for this system treats the two bots as specialized agents that share one student model rather than two isolated tools, mirroring published architectures for adaptive e-learning. The INCA architecture uses a personal agent that stays aware of each learner's characteristics and coordinates a set of expert agents such as assessment agents and help agents, closely resembling a Content bot and Coach bot both reading from and writing to one shared profile. A similar pattern extends Moodle with an intelligent "instructional decision" agent that collects information generated by other agents and uses it to produce personalized support for students and tutors, which is the coordination layer needed between the two bots. The Content bot's job is to consume the student's weak topics, quiz results, and time-on-page signals, then select easier or harder lessons; systems like MAEL combine a multi-agent layer with ontologies and neural networks to build personalized learning paths and let learners proceed at their own pace. The Coach bot's job is to consume that same student profile plus the Content bot's latest path change, then decide whether to give encouragement, a remedial quiz, or an advanced challenge, and the two bots stay synchronized by reading and writing to one shared record rather than only messaging each other. The simplest workable coordination rule is close to what you proposed: define one shared trigger value, such as quiz score, and let both bots react to changes in it, similar to how learning-management "adaptive release" rules make an item's availability depend on whether a grade is less than, greater than, equal to, or between specified values. That same system shows how conditions combine, since a single rule can require quiz score AND group membership together, while separate rules combine with OR logic, so one rule releases remedial material for low scorers and another releases advanced material for high scorers. Applied here, a workable first version is: if a topic-level quiz score falls below 50%, the Content bot swaps in an easier video for that topic, and this same score-drop event tells the Coach bot to queue a short remedial quiz once the student finishes the new content. Conversely, if a student scores above roughly 80% on two consecutive quizzes for a topic, the Content bot should advance them to harder material, and the Coach bot should switch to a lighter confidence check, so both bots always react to the same score-crossing event. Before building this around a "learning style" input, be cautious, since a rigorous review found no credible evidence that matching instructional method to a student's claimed learning style improves outcomes, because the pattern required to prove it -- one method working best for one style and a different method working best for another -- essentially never appears in well-designed studies. That does not make learning-style data useless as a minor signal, but the system should not rely on it as the primary rule the way it relies on quiz scores and time-on-page. For setting the "50%" cutoff, intelligent-tutoring research frames mastery thresholds as a tunable trade-off, since a threshold that is too lenient creates false positives where an unmastered student is judged to have mastered a skill, while one too strict creates false negatives that force extra unneeded practice. Mastery-based approaches have shown real benefit historically, particularly for lower-performing students, supporting an easier-video and remedial-quiz rule targeted at students below the cutoff rather than uniform extra practice for everyone. For measuring whether the system works, two evidence-grounded metrics fit directly: topic-level quiz score improvement after remediation, and course completion rate, where published MOOC data shows completion rates ranging from 0.7% to 52.1% with a median around 12.6%, and shows the first two weeks are the most critical window for engagement. That same analysis found automated assessment is associated with higher completion than peer grading, a useful sanity check that the Coach bot's automated quizzing is a reasonable design choice. To test this before a full rollout, run a small implementation pilot, an explicit method for trying a new program in a small sample of real classrooms and gathering data before broader investment, matching the instinct to "just try with a small class." When running that pilot, keep it small, include a comparison group of students who do not get the adaptive bots so gains can be attributed to the system, and maintain open communication with the teacher throughout. A lighter alternative is the small-scale mini-randomized trial used by education researchers, deliberately time- and cost-efficient, with results aggregated later into a larger evidence base once several runs are complete. For the "bad recommendation and scores go down" scenario, build the same mastery-threshold logic into a safety check: track each student's score trend after every Content-bot change, and if scores drop for two consecutive interactions after a path change, automatically roll the student back to their previous path and flag the case instead of pushing further changes. This rollback rule directly extends the false-positive framing above, since a sustained score drop is strong evidence the system made a false-positive mastery call and should self-correct rather than persist. For teacher override, government guidance on AI in education explicitly recommends keeping teachers "in the loop and in control," requiring that they understand the model well enough to knowingly use, modify, or override its recommendations for individual students. The same report warns against uncritical trust in automated advice, citing an experiment where people followed a robot's directions during a simulated emergency even after being told the robot was broken, a strong argument for a visible, low-friction override control. Practically, this means giving the teacher dashboard a one-click "pause adaptive path" toggle per student and a way to manually set the next lesson or quiz, since override capability is described as essential because teachers understand context the bots do not. The same source stresses that AI recommendations should be explainable and inspectable, so surfacing each bot's reason for a change in plain language next to the override button closes the loop between automated adaptation and human control.

Research request:

I want to make an ai system with a few bots that work together to make personalized learning paths for students i'm thinking we need two bots. a 'Content bot' that finds lessons based on what a student is bad at, and a 'Coach bot' that gives feedback and practice quizzes. they need to look at data like quiz results, time spent on a page, maybe their learning style? and we need to figure out how they work together. eg when the content bot changes the student's path, how does the coach bot know to give them a remedial quiz or something describe the main logic. it doesn't have to be super complex. just a simple rule for how they adapt over time. For exmaple 'if student quiz score < 50%, content bot finds an easier video' how do i even know if it works? I need a couple metrics (eg improving quiz scores or more people finish the course). and how can I test it? maybe a simulation or just try with a small class. I also need a plan for when it gives a bad recommendation, and the student's scores go down? and how can a human teacher step in and take over/override it?

adaptive learning system rule based remediation quiz score threshold

Overview
The Adaptive Release functionality of LearnJCU allows teaching staff to control availability of content using criteria to allow or deny access to items such as lecture materials and quizzes. It cannot be applied to menu items or tools such as Announcements and Discussion Forums.
You can control the availability of content based on a set of rules you create with the following release criteria:
Date: Release an item only on a specified date or time. Options include: on a exact date, until a certain date, or during a defined period of time.
Membership: Release an item to specific users or groups of users (eg. Students in a particular tute group)
Grade: Release an item if a specified graded item was attempted or users received a certain score—less than, greater than, equal to, or between. You can also release an item based on a calculated column in the Grade Centre
Review status: . Release an item when another content item is marked as reviewed.
Examples of use
Some examples where Adaptive Release has been usefully applied include:
Grouping students based on prior knowledge, and providing different, or additional, material to the more experienced
Providing a professional example of an assignment to students who have completed that assignment
Making a complex text visible once students have reviewed an introductory text
Providing different material for different project groups to work on
Providing advanced material for those who scored high on a test
Providing remedial material for those who scored low on a test.
Frequently Asked Questions
Q.Can you use multiple criteria in an Adaptive Release rule? A. Yes. Adding multiple criteria within a single rule means that all set criteria must be met for the rule to be satisfied and the item to be available. For example, if a single rule requires a quiz score of 7 AND membership in Group A then both criteria must be met to make the content available.
Q. Can you apply multiple Adaptive Release rules to a single item? A. Yes. If you apply multiple rules to a single item then at least one of the rules must be satisfied for the item to be available. For example, if Rule 1 requires a quiz score of 7 and Rule 2 requires membership in Group A then either Rule 1 OR Rule 2 may be met to make the content available.

A practical design for this system starts by treating the two bots as specialized agents that share one student model rather than two isolated tools, which mirrors published architectures for adaptive e-learning.

The INCA architecture, for example, uses a personal agent that stays aware of each learner's characteristics and coordinates a set of expert agents such as assessment agents and help agents, which is a close analogue to your Content bot and Coach bot both reading from and writing to one shared profile.

[shard_02234_67298]
A similar pattern extends Moodle with an intelligent "instructional decision" agent that collects information generated by the other agents and uses it to produce the best personalized support for students and tutors, which is the coordination layer your system needs between Content bot and Coach bot.

[shard_01716_79806]
The Content bot's job is to consume the student's weak topics, quiz results, and time-on-page signals, and select easier or harder lessons; systems like MAEL combine a multi-agent layer with ontologies and neural networks specifically to build personalized learning paths guided by educational goals and to let learners proceed at their own pace.

[shard_00573_5867]
The Coach bot's job is to consume the same student profile plus the Content bot's latest path change, then decide whether to give encouragement, a remedial quiz, or an advanced challenge; the two bots stay synchronized by both reading and writing to that one shared student record rather than passing messages only to each other.

The simplest working coordination rule is exactly the kind you proposed: define one shared trigger value, such as quiz score, and let both bots react to changes in it, similar to how learning-management "adaptive release" rules let an item's availability depend on whether a grade is less than, greater than, equal to, or between specified values.

[shard_05629_28067]
That same system shows how to combine conditions, since a single rule can require quiz score AND group membership to both be true, while separate rules can be combined with OR logic, so one rule releases remedial material for low scorers and another releases advanced material for high scorers.

[shard_05629_28067]
Applied to your two bots, a workable first version is: if a topic-level quiz score falls below 50%, the Content bot swaps in an easier video or worked example for that topic, and this same score-drop event fires a second rule that tells the Coach bot to immediately queue a short remedial quiz on that same topic once the student finishes the new content.

Conversely, if the student scores above roughly 80% on two consecutive quizzes for a topic, the Content bot should advance them to harder material, and the Coach bot's rule should switch from remedial quizzing to a lighter "confidence check" quiz, so the two bots always react to the same score-crossing event rather than needing bot-to-bot negotiation.

Before building this around a "learning style" input, be cautious: a rigorous review found no credible evidence that matching instructional method to a student's claimed learning style improves outcomes, because the required experimental pattern -- one method working best for one style and a different method working best for another -- essentially never appears in well-designed studies.

[shard_01831_41519]
That does not mean learning-style data is useless as a personalization signal, but it means the system should not rely on it as the primary rule for choosing content the way it relies on quiz scores and time-on-page.

[shard_01831_41519]
For deciding exactly where to set your "50%" cutoff, intelligent-tutoring research frames it as a tunable trade-off: a mastery threshold that is too lenient creates false positives where an unmastered student is judged to have mastered a skill, while a threshold that is too strict creates false negatives where a student who already knows the material is forced through unnecessary extra practice.

[shard_04377_7608]
Mastery-based approaches have shown real benefit historically, and research reviews note that they are particularly helpful for lower-performing students, which supports using an easier-video/remedial-quiz rule specifically for students below the cutoff rather than applying extra practice uniformly to everyone.

[shard_02427_29645]
For measuring whether the whole system works, two evidence-grounded metrics fit your idea directly: topic-level quiz score improvement after remediation, and course completion rate, where published MOOC data shows completion rates ranging from 0.7% to 52.1% with a median around 12.6%, and shows that the first two weeks are the most critical window for engagement and assessment submission.

[shard_01311_63745]
That same analysis found automated assessment is associated with higher completion than peer grading, which is a useful sanity check that your Coach bot's automated quizzing approach is a reasonable design choice rather than a risk factor for completion.

[shard_01311_63745]

[shard_02199_55562]

[shard_04017_73072]
If a full pilot feels too heavy, a lighter-weight alternative used by education researchers is the small-scale mini-randomized trial, which is deliberately time- and cost-efficient and can be aggregated later into a larger evidence base once you have several runs.

[shard_04377_7608]
This rollback rule is the direct extension of the false-positive/false-negative framing above, since a sustained score drop is strong evidence the system made a false-positive mastery call and should self-correct rather than persist.
